newsitem.title: USA: MGM management completes $1.3 billion buyout.
newsitem.headline: MGM management completes $1.3 billion buyout.

text.p: A management-led group of executives, including billionaire Kirk Kerkorian, finalized its $1.3 billion acquisition of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc. Thursday, ending a dismal chapter in the film studio's storied history.

The group acquired MGM from France's state-owned Consortium de Realisation, a holding company formed to dispose of several assets of France's Credit Lyonnais which became the owner of the studio under a bailout plan for the bank.

Credit Lyonnais had taken over MGM from Italian financier Giancarlo Parretti, who bought it in 1990 and later defaulted on loans. Just last week, Parretti was convicted of perjury in Delaware court in conjunction with his purchase of MGM.
The studio, founded in 1924, has produced some of the film industry's most acclaimed movies and enduring characters, such as "West Side Story," "Raging Bull" and 17 James Bond films.
Moreover, its famed "Leo the Lion" trademark is one of the most recognized brands in the world.
"This company has survived through some very difficult times because of its brand name," MGM Chairman Frank Mancuso told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Indeed, brand recognition is currently at a premium in Hollywood because executivess see it as the key to opening up global markets.

Following that line of thinking, the new management team will quickly move to exploit branding by launching lines of merchandise based on the trademark and charaters such as Bond and The Pink Panther.

On the film front, Mancuso said MGM has slated production of some 13 to 14 films between now and the end of 1997, including a new Bond movie for next year. He also looks to acquire between three and four films for MGM in the next year.
Since Mancuso took MGM's reins in 1993, the studio has seen the successful distribution of films like "Leaving Las Vegas," "The Birdcage" and "Goldeneye," a James Bond film.

Mancuso's first move in the film department will be to replace John Calley, president of MGM's United Artists production wing, by mid-November when Calley will resign to be co-president at Sony Corp.'s Sony Pictures Entertainment.
For working capital, Mancuso has about $350 million from a loan syndicate formed as part of the acquisition. Financial analysts believe he will need nearly twice that amount to jump start production.

Mancuso said he will have cash flow of between $600 million to $700 million over the next four to five years to help fuel new film, television and other projects. He also noted other avenues to raise funds.
"One thing you can consider for the future is an initial public offering of stock," Mancuso said, though he provided no timetable for such a move.

The deal to acquire MGM was sealed in a bidding process that ended in July when Kerkorian's Tracinda Corp. and Australian media conglomerate Seven Network Ltd. offered their support for Mancuso's executive team.

Kerkorian has owned the studio twice before in its history, and his group is hopeful it can find synergy between the studio and the MGM Grand Inc. casino in Las Vegas, of which Kerkorian owns the majority.

Seven Network will use its stake in the studio to get its foot in the door of the burgeoning global entertainment business and to provide programming for its core broadcast television business in Australia and the Asia Pacific region.
